commits.author: Giulio Ardoino
commits.subject: fix: say when the hosted PWA cannot reach the server, and cover the question defaults
commits.body:
#70 publishes the web app over HTTPS, and an HTTPS page may not talk to an `http://`
address unless that address is loopback. Measured in a browser against one server bound to
0.0.0.0:4096: `http://127.0.0.1:4096` and `http://localhost:4096` answered 200, the same
server on `http://192.168.1.64:4096` was refused before the request left. That is the
phone-to-PC setup the app exists for, and all the user saw was `Failed to fetch` — no
`--cors` change can help, because the server is never reached.

- `isMixedContentBlocked` names the case, and Settings shows it next to the host field
  instead of waiting for a connection test that cannot pass. Loopback in all its
  spellings, an `https://` server and a half-typed host stay quiet.
- The native build is excluded explicitly: it reaches the server through CapacitorHttp,
  not the WebView, so the restriction never applies whatever `androidScheme` serves the
  bundle under.
- README now spells out the limitation and the four ways around it, instead of implying
  that listing the Pages origin in `--cors` is all it takes.

The service worker's revalidating cache writes were started inside the response chain,
where the worker may be terminated before they land; the event keeps them alive now.

#69 shipped without tests. Its central claim checks out against the tool it mirrors: the
question tool's own parameter schema has no `custom` field at all, so a question always
arrives with it undefined and the documented default of `true` applies — reading it for
truthiness hid the free-text answer on every question ever asked. Pinned, along with the
single-answer clearing and the answers-are-arrays-of-labels shape the highlighting needs.

web: clean build and typecheck, 6/6 suites. bridge: 43/43. Host field measured at 375x812
and 800: no horizontal overflow, the explanation takes the full grid row.

commits.author: Giulio Ardoino
commits.subject: ci: deploy the hosted web app from release tags, not from main
commits.body:
The APK is compiled on every push to main but published only on a `v*` tag. The Pages
workflow arrived with no such gate: `push` on `main` filtered by `paths: web/**`, so the
public web app would have tracked the tip of the branch while the public APK tracked
releases — two channels telling users two different versions of the truth, and every merge
live with nothing in between. It now triggers on the same `v*` tags, with
`workflow_dispatch` kept for a manual redeploy.

Publishing to users also deserves the same gate the APK release has, so the job runs the
six web suites instead of the type-check alone.

Workflow YAML re-parsed after the change: triggers are `workflow_dispatch` and `push` on
`v*`, and the build job keeps its step order with the suites ahead of the build.

commits.subject: docs: bring the README back in line with three harnesses and the current app
commits.body:
"configure and test connection to a supported harness (OpenCode server or OMP bridge)"
listed two of the three backends, eleven lines under a table that lists all three. The same
omission sat in the technology stack, which described the bridge as the OMP bridge when it
fronts PI as well.

Fixing only those two would have left the sections around them describing an older app.
What It Can Do never mentioned answering the agent's questions, model or agent selection,
changed files and diffs, session rename and delete, choosing a working directory, or the
theme switch — most of a release's worth of features. Per-harness support is stated against
`backendCapabilities.ts` and `harness-profiles.js` rather than asserted, and split into what
works everywhere and what depends on the backend, since the app hides what a harness cannot
do.

App Configuration still told everyone to use port 4096 with "credentials used to start
OpenCode server"; the bridge listens on 4097. Main Endpoints Used listed seven paths out of
the fifteen the app calls, and none of the bridge's own, so it now matches `api.ts` and
points at docs/DEPENDENCIES.md for what sits behind them.

Claims are deliberately narrower than they could be in one place: the composer lets you type
a follow-up while the agent works, and the bridge queues it for OMP and PI, but I did not
verify that an OpenCode server queues rather than interleaves, so the shared list says what
the UI does and stops there.

commits.subject: ci: keep the curated release notes, and fail loudly when they are missing
commits.body:
v2.4.0 published with the full changelog link, no changes listed and no contributors
named — the one outcome the credit convention exists to prevent. Two independent causes,
both silent.

`actions/checkout` writes the tag ref pointing at the commit rather than at the tag
object, so the annotation is absent from the clone even at `fetch-depth: 0`. Verified
after the fact: the ref on the remote is type `tag` and its message still holds all 28
lines, so nothing was lost in the tag — only in the checkout. `git describe` accepts a
lightweight tag, which is why the changelog link appeared and made the release look
merely terse rather than broken. `git fetch --tags --force` restores the objects.

An empty summary was then tolerated on the grounds that a terse release beats a failed
one. It does not: a failure costs a re-run, while this cost a published release that
credited nobody and was only noticed by reading it. The step now fails and says how to
re-cut the tag.

Both paths exercised locally against v2.4.0 with the workflow's own shell: the annotation
produces all four headings, and a lightweight tag trips the guard.

`git tag -a -F` also strips every `#` line as a comment under git's default cleanup, which
deletes the two `##` headings the format in CONTRIBUTING.md mandates — that is how this
tag was written in the first place. Documented with `--cleanup=verbatim` and a one-line
check to run before pushing.
